items.title: gRPC-over-binder — the `SecurityPolicy` is the caller check, not the manifest
items.vrt: `broken_access_control.privilege_escalation` (varies); `sensitive_data_exposure.disclosure_of_secrets.for_publicly_accessible_asset` (P1) on what the RPCs return
items.applies_to: Google/GMS-family apps and anything using grpc-binder
items.maps_to: Local senior-researcher corpus, gRPC-over-binder section; MASWE-0018
items.test:
A `<service android:exported="true">` with `<action android:name="grpc.io.action.BIND"/>` and
**no** manifest permission looks alarming and is usually fine — the gate is the server's
`SecurityPolicy`, evaluated at the RPC layer. **`onBind` succeeds either way, so a successful bind proves
nothing.** Trace the policy before rating anything.
items.how:
```bash
grep -n 'grpc.io.action.BIND' $DEC/apktool/AndroidManifest.xml
grep -rn 'SecurityPolicy\|securityPolicy\|permitAll\|getPackagesForUid\|hasSignature\|isGoogleSigned' $DEC/jadx/sources/
# the policy is usually built deep in the Dagger graph, not inline — follow the provider
grep -rn 'getSecurityPolicy\|Provider<.*SecurityPolicy>\|@Provides.*SecurityPolicy' $DEC/jadx/sources/
```
The robust pattern to look for: resolve the caller uid → `pm.getPackagesForUid(uid)` → require the
package to be in an **explicit allow-list** AND the caller to be **Google-signed**, denying by default
when the allow-list is empty.
items.proof:
The `SecurityPolicy` implementation body, quoted by `file:line`. The bug is a policy that is
`permitAll()`, checks only a **package name** without a signature check, or is constructed empty.
Record every traced policy as a negative or candidate with the `file:line` of the concrete `SecurityPolicy`;
do not carry negatives between engagements — the policy is rebuilt per release.
items.escalation:
Enumerate the RPC surface and re-run D15 authorisation tests against each method.
Dynamic confirmation needs a real gRPC-binder client — you cannot craft one from adb, so when you rely
on the code trace alone, **say so in the report**.
items.ruled_out_when:
The traced policy requires both an explicit allow-list membership and a signature
check, denies by default on an empty list, and you have followed the DI provider to the concrete object
rather than reading an interface.

items.title: Privileged listener service declared **without** its `BIND_*` permission
items.vrt: `broken_access_control.privilege_escalation` (varies) — rated on what the callback accepts
items.applies_to: All. Declaration-side issue, independent of targetSdk.
items.maps_to: MASWE-0018 (Lack of Authentication or Authorization on App Components); MASVS-PLATFORM; Oversecured banking write-up "AIDL Interface Abuse — service exposes AIDL interface performing auth operations without validating calling UID/package"
items.test:
This is "validates the action but never the caller" in its purest form. A listener service is
written on the assumption that its only caller is `system_server`; the bind permission is what makes
that true. The docs state the `BIND_*` permission "strictly enforces that only the system can bind to
your service". Remove it and any app can bind and drive the callback directly with objects it
fabricated.
items.how:
```bash
grep -nE 'android\.accessibilityservice\.AccessibilityService|android\.service\.notification\.NotificationListenerService|android\.service\.autofill\.AutofillService|android\.service\.quicksettings\.action\.QS_TILE|android\.service\.credentials\.CredentialProviderService|android\.nfc\.cardemulation\.action\.(HOST|OFF_HOST)_APDU_SERVICE|android\.companion\.CompanionDeviceService|android\.telecom\.(InCallService|ConnectionService|CallScreeningService|CallRedirectionService)|android\.service\.controls\.ControlsProviderService|android\.service\.dreams\.DreamService|android\.printservice\.PrintService|android\.intent\.action\.TTS_SERVICE|android\.service\.voice|android\.service\.chooser\.ChooserTargetService|androidx\.car\.app\.CarAppService|com\.google\.android\.gms\.wearable\.(BIND_LISTENER|MESSAGE_RECEIVED|DATA_CHANGED)|android\.app\.slice\.category\.SLICE' "$DEC/apktool/AndroidManifest.xml"
```
For each hit, read **upward** to the enclosing `<service>` and record whether the matching permission is
present: `BIND_ACCESSIBILITY_SERVICE`, `BIND_NOTIFICATION_LISTENER_SERVICE`, `BIND_AUTOFILL_SERVICE`,
`BIND_QUICK_SETTINGS_TILE`, `BIND_CREDENTIAL_PROVIDER_SERVICE` (API 34), `BIND_NFC_SERVICE`,
`BIND_COMPANION_DEVICE_SERVICE`, `BIND_INCALL_SERVICE`, `BIND_TELECOM_CONNECTION_SERVICE`, `BIND_SCREENING_SERVICE`,
`BIND_CALL_REDIRECTION_SERVICE`, `BIND_CONTROLS`, `BIND_DREAM_SERVICE`, `BIND_PRINT_SERVICE`, `BIND_TEXT_SERVICE`,
`BIND_CHOOSER_TARGET_SERVICE`. Then bind from a zero-permission app with the
declared action and drive the interface:
```java
Intent i = new Intent("android.service.notification.NotificationListenerService")
        .setPackage("com.target.app");
bindService(i, conn, Context.BIND_AUTO_CREATE);
```
and check the handler:
```bash
grep -rnE 'Binder\.getCallingUid|getCallingPackage|getPackagesForUid|checkCallingPermission|enforceCallingPermission' $DEC/jadx/sources/
```
items.proof:
A `<service>` with the listener `<intent-filter>`, `android:exported="true"` and **no**
`android:permission="android.permission.BIND_*"`, plus a non-null `IBinder` arriving in your PoC's
`onServiceConnected`, plus a method call that returns data or mutates state. Capture the returned
object in the attacker app's log.
items.escalation:
Whatever the callback does with the `AccessibilityEvent` / `StatusBarNotification` /
`FillRequest` it now accepts from you — token extraction → D15; OTP → D13.
An unguarded `HostApduService` accepts attacker APDUs (→ D23 payment flow); an unguarded
`CredentialProviderService` answers `BeginGetCredentialRequest` for any package (→ D13 passkey disclosure).
items.ruled_out_when:
Every listener `<service>` carries its matching `BIND_*` permission **and** the
handler additionally checks `Binder.getCallingUid()` — the permission alone leaves the app trusting a
system caller it never verifies, which matters the moment the app is also installed on an OEM build
where that permission is held by more than `system_server`.

items.title: The app's own `AccessibilityService`, and the app's exposure to someone else's
items.vrt: `broken_authentication_and_session_management.authentication_bypass` (P1) when screen scrape plus gesture injection completes a transaction
items.attacker: AM-04 (the user must enable the service — a single user action, not an exploit)
items.applies_to: All. `accessibilityDataSensitive` (`View.setAccessibilityDataSensitive`, `android:accessibilityDataSensitive`) is **API 34+**; `android:filterTouchesWhenObscured="true"` implies it from API 34. It hides nodes only from services that do not declare `android:isAccessibilityTool="true"` — a sideloaded service can declare it, so it is a Play-policy control, not a security boundary; `FLAG_SECURE` is the only hard one.
items.maps_to: `guide/topics/ui/accessibility/service` (`canRetrieveWindowContent`, `canPerformGestures`, `dispatchGesture`, `AccessibilityNodeInfo.performAction`); `privacy-and-security/risks/tapjacking`; ATT&CK T1513 (Screen Capture), T1516 (Input Injection), T1663 (Remote Access Software); MASWE-0039
items.test:
Two directions. (a) If the *target* ships an `AccessibilityService`, check the declaration and
the bind permission (D06-046) and read what its callbacks do with events it is handed. (b) The
higher-value direction for a banking or payments app: the target's **missing mitigations** against a
third-party accessibility service — no `FLAG_SECURE` on sensitive screens, no `accessibilityDataSensitive`,
no `filterTouchesWhenObscured`. Scope this honestly: the user must enable your service, so the finding
is the victim app's exposure, not a platform bug.

```bash
grep -rn 'canRetrieveWindowContent\|canPerformGestures\|dispatchGesture' $DEC/apktool/res/xml/ $DEC/jadx/sources/
grep -rn 'accessibilityDataSensitive\|FLAG_SECURE\|filterTouchesWhenObscured' $DEC/jadx/sources/ $DEC/apktool/res/layout/
adb shell settings get secure enabled_accessibility_services
```
Build a stub a11y service with `canRetrieveWindowContent` and dump the victim's tree:
```java
AccessibilityNodeInfo root = getRootInActiveWindow();
// walk and log every getText() / getContentDescription()
```
items.proof:
Your stub logging the victim's PIN entry, balance or OTP text, and — with
`canPerformGestures` — `dispatchGesture()` completing a transfer. Video plus the log, with the
precondition sentence ("the user enabled the service") stated in the report.
items.escalation: Full session and transaction control; → D04 UI redress, → D13.
items.ruled_out_when:
The sensitive screens set `FLAG_SECURE` (so the node tree is unreadable), or the
transaction-authorising controls set `accessibilityDataSensitive`/`filterTouchesWhenObscured` on API 34+
**and** your stub service, declared `isAccessibilityTool="true"`, still gets empty text — state which of the
two held. Prove it by running the dump and getting empty text.

items.vrt: `broken_authentication_and_session_management.two_fa_bypass` (P3) at the VRT default; request P1 `authentication_bypass` when the captured OTP completes an account takeover end to end

The OTP or message body in your stub's logcat with the victim package named, and/or a
captured `contentIntent` successfully `send()`-ed with an attacker `fillIn`. Cancel the notification
afterwards to show the user never sees it — that is what turns "read" into "intercept".

items.title: `androidx.startup.InitializationProvider` — the pre-authentication code path nobody wrote
items.vrt: `sensitive_data_exposure.disclosure_of_secrets.pii_leakage_exposure` (varies); the install-collision variant is availability only

items.maps_to: `topic/libraries/app-startup` (provider XML, authority format `${applicationId}.androidx-startup`, documented `android:exported="false"`); MASWE-0069

Every `<meta-data android:name="com.example.SomeInitializer" android:value="androidx.startup" />`
names a class that runs in `InitializationProvider.onCreate()` — **before the launcher Activity, before

```bash
grep -nB2 -A2 'androidx.startup' $DEC/apktool/AndroidManifest.xml
adb shell dumpsys package com.target.app | sed -n '/Provider Resolver Table/,/^$/p'
# read each named initializer
```

```bash
adb shell dumpsys package providers | grep androidx-startup
```

items.title: `JobService` missing `BIND_JOB_SERVICE`
items.vrt: `broken_access_control.privilege_escalation` (varies)
items.applies_to: All apps using `JobScheduler` or WorkManager (which contributes `SystemJobService`)
items.maps_to: `reference/android/app/job/JobScheduler` (`BIND_JOB_SERVICE`, `setPersisted` + `RECEIVE_BOOT_COMPLETED`, `setExtras` persisted vs `setTransientExtras` in-memory); `about/versions/14/behavior-changes-14` (`ACCESS_NETWORK_STATE` now required for `setRequiredNetworkType()`/`setRequiredNetwork()` or `SecurityException`; ANR on `onStartJob`/`onStopJob` overrun); MASWE-0018

`JobScheduler` requires `android:permission="android.permission.BIND_JOB_SERVICE"` on the

calls `onStartJob(JobParameters)` with parameters it fabricated — including the job's extras.

```bash
  | grep -n -A4 -iE 'androidx.work|InitializationProvider|SystemJobService|RescheduleReceiver|DiagnosticsReceiver|BIND_JOB_SERVICE|extends.*JobService'
grep -rn 'extends JobService\|onStartJob\|onStopJob' $DEC/jadx/sources/ -A20
adb shell dumpsys jobscheduler | grep -A15 com.target.app
```

```bash
adb shell dumpsys jobscheduler | grep -A15 com.target.app
adb shell am broadcast -n com.target.app/androidx.work.diagnostics.DiagnosticsReceiver
```

A `JobService` in the merged manifest with `exported="true"` (or an intent filter) and no

Every `JobService` in the merged manifest declares `BIND_JOB_SERVICE` — check the

items.title: `androidx.work.multiprocess` — `RemoteWorkerService` is a bound service with a parcel boundary
items.vrt: `broken_access_control.privilege_escalation` (varies)

Multiprocess WorkManager exposes a bound service so one process can enqueue work in another.
Two questions: is that service exported in the merged manifest, and does the app pass its **own**

framework parcel-mismatch bug class — validate in one process, execute in another)?
items.how:
```bash
grep -n 'android:process' $DEC/apktool/AndroidManifest.xml
grep -rn 'androidx.work.multiprocess\|RemoteWorkManager\|RemoteListenableWorker\|RemoteWorkerService' $DEC/jadx/sources/ $DEC/apktool/AndroidManifest.xml
grep -rln 'implements Parcelable' $DEC/jadx/sources/ | xargs grep -ln 'catch'
```

The service's manifest entry showing `exported="true"` with no permission, plus a bind from a
zero-permission app; or, for the mismatch variant, `Parcel.dataPosition()` after `createFromParcel`

items.title: `JobIntentService` entry points — LEGACY, and still the enqueue path in old builds

```bash
grep -nB4 -A10 'JobIntentService\|BIND_JOB_SERVICE' $DEC/apktool/AndroidManifest.xml

```

items.title: A security decision implemented as a `oneway` transaction
items.vrt: `broken_authentication_and_session_management.failure_to_invalidate_session.on_logout` (P4) when a "revoke"/"logout" call can be dropped; `broken_access_control.privilege_escalation` (varies) when the dropped call is a lock or entitlement revocation
items.attacker: AM-03 (must be able to interpose, typically via D06-042) or AM-08
items.applies_to: All
items.maps_to: AOSP "Binder threading" — one-way calls return immediately; ordering is guaranteed only within a single interface; the driver reserves a separate async area. `android.os.Binder.FLAG_ONEWAY`.
items.test:
A `oneway` call returns immediately and the caller learns nothing about success. Security-
relevant state changes implemented as `oneway` cannot be confirmed by the caller and can be silently
dropped — so the caller's code continues on the success path with the state unchanged.
items.proof:
The caller proceeding down its success path (UI shows "signed out", the log says "revoked")
while the server-side state is unchanged — demonstrated by a subsequent authenticated request
succeeding.
items.escalation:
→ D13 (a session that survives logout); pair with D06-064 for a targeted denial of the
async transaction space.
items.ruled_out_when:
Every security-relevant state change is a synchronous transaction whose return value
the caller checks, or the state change is confirmed by a subsequent read — show the read.

items.title: Transaction-buffer exhaustion and a fail-open `TransactionTooLargeException` catch
items.vrt: `application_level_denial_of_service_dos.high_impact_and_or_medium_difficulty` (P3) for the availability effect; `broken_access_control.privilege_escalation` (varies) when the exception path is a fail-open branch
items.applies_to: All
items.maps_to: `android.os.TransactionTooLargeException` javadoc: "The Binder transaction buffer has a limited fixed size, currently 1MB, which is shared by all transactions in progress for the process… this exception can be thrown when there are many transactions in progress even when most of the individual transactions are of moderate size."
items.test:
The transaction buffer is a fixed ~1 MB region **shared by all in-flight transactions of a
process**. An attacker who can make the target hold many or large transactions makes unrelated,
legitimate transactions in that process fail. The finding is rarely the DoS — it is what the app's
`catch` block does.
items.how:
```bash
grep -rn 'TransactionTooLargeException\|catch (RemoteException\|DeadObjectException' $DEC/jadx/sources/ -A8
```
Drive it against an exported method taking a `byte[]`/`String`/`Bundle`:
```java
byte[] big = new byte[900 * 1024];
for (int i = 0; i < 8; i++)
    new Thread(() -> { try { svc.method(big); } catch (Throwable t) { Log.w("POC", "" + t); } }).start();
```
```bash
adb logcat | grep -E 'TransactionTooLarge|!!! FAILED BINDER TRANSACTION'
```
items.proof:
The logcat failures, **plus** the app's catch block falling through to an insecure default —
skipping a check, returning cached data, or treating the failure as "allowed". An entitlement check that
`return true` on `RemoteException` is the shape to hunt.
items.escalation: The fail-open branch → whatever the check guarded → D13/D23.
items.ruled_out_when:
Every `catch (RemoteException|TransactionTooLargeException)` fails closed (returns
the denied value or rethrows), read from the decompiled body.

items.title: A `ParcelFileDescriptor` returned over binder is a live FD in your process
items.vrt: `server_side_injection.file_inclusion.local` (P1) for a sandbox-crossing read; `server_side_injection.remote_code_execution_rce` (P1) when the FD is writable and the file is later loaded
items.applies_to: All
items.maps_to: AOSP "Binder IPC" (a `Parcel` carries active objects — binder references and file descriptors); `ParcelFileDescriptor` as the standard AIDL FD carrier; MASTG-TEST-0007 (deprecated)
items.test:
A service returning a `ParcelFileDescriptor` hands the caller a kernel FD with whatever access
mode it was opened with. Look for FDs opened `MODE_READ_WRITE` on a file the caller should only read,
FDs onto a directory or a `/proc` path, and FDs that outlive the intended operation.
items.how:
```bash
grep -rnE 'ParcelFileDescriptor\.(open|dup|adoptFd|fromSocket|createPipe)|writeFileDescriptor|openFileDescriptor|MODE_READ_WRITE|MODE_WORLD' $DEC/jadx/sources/
# after the bind + call, inspect what you were handed
adb shell ls -l /proc/$(adb shell pidof com.poc.attacker)/fd/
```
items.proof:
`ls -l /proc/<attacker pid>/fd/` showing a symlink into `/data/data/com.target.app/…` that
your UID could never `open()` directly, plus a successful `read()` (and, for the writable case, a
`write()`) through that FD with the bytes shown.
items.escalation:
A writable FD into the app's own data directory is a stored-injection primitive — write
a `.dex`/`.jar` the app loads (→ D17) or overwrite a config the app trusts (→ D11).
items.ruled_out_when:
Every returned FD is opened read-only on a file whose contents the caller could
already obtain, or the method returns no FD at all — list the methods you checked.

items.title: The app's own `Parcelable` has a `writeToParcel`/`createFromParcel` mismatch
items.vrt: `broken_access_control.privilege_escalation` (varies); Critical when it turns a validated object into a different one after the boundary
items.applies_to: Any app that passes its own `Parcelable`s across a process boundary — a `:remote` service, multiprocess WorkManager, widget `RemoteViews`, or AIDL
items.maps_to: michalbednarski/ReparcelBug2 — **CVE-2021-0928** ("a `writeToParcel`/`createFromParcel` serialization mismatch in `OutputConfiguration`"); michalbednarski/LeakValue — **CVE-2022-20452**; michalbednarski/TheLastBundleMismatch — **CVE-2023-45777** (bypass of Android 13's Lazy Bundle mitigation because `AccountManagerService.checkKeyIntent()` used the untyped `bundle.getParcelable(KEY_INTENT)`); MASWE-0050
items.test:
Owned by D08-029 (the Parcelable write/read mismatch test) — run it against every Parcelable that crosses the app's own process boundary (D06-061) and record under D08-029; this row keeps only the `:remote`/multiprocess-WorkManager application. It is the `Parcelable` implementation's responsibility to ensure `createFromParcel` reads the
same number of bytes `writeToParcel` wrote. When they diverge — a `catch` in `createFromParcel` that
swallows an exception mid-read, or a field added to the writer and not the reader — the unread bytes are
interpreted as the *next* object, and an attacker who controls one field smuggles a different object
into a later field, past whatever validation ran in between.
items.how:
```bash
grep -rln 'implements Parcelable\|: Parcelable' $DEC/jadx/sources/ | while read f; do
  echo "== $f"
  sed -n '/writeToParcel/,/}/p' "$f" | grep -cE 'write[A-Z][A-Za-z]*\('
  sed -n '/createFromParcel/,/}/p;/protected .*(Parcel/,/}/p' "$f" | grep -cE 'read[A-Z][A-Za-z]*\('
done
# the four warning signs from ReparcelBug2
grep -rn 'createFromParcel' $DEC/jadx/sources/ -A25 | grep -nE 'catch\s*\(|readList\(|readParcelable\(|readBundle\(|readSerializable\('
```
A write-count differing from the read-count for the same class, or a `catch` that does not rethrow, is
the candidate.
items.proof:
In a harness, write the class to a `Parcel` and read it back: `Parcel.dataPosition()` after
`createFromParcel` differing from `dataSize()` proves the mismatch. Then demonstrate that a following
field in the same `Bundle` decodes to an attacker-chosen value, with `getClass()` differing on each side.
items.escalation: → D17; in an app this bypasses whatever the validating process checked.
items.ruled_out_when:
Read and write counts match for every app-defined `Parcelable`, no
`createFromParcel` swallows an exception, and untyped `readParcelable`/`getParcelable` calls are replaced
with the class-constrained forms.

items.title: `isolatedProcess` — a real containment boundary, in both directions
items.severity_note: Medium — standalone; it is the amplifier for a D16 memory-safety finding
items.vrt: n/a standalone — it modifies the rating of a memory-safety finding
items.applies_to: Android 4.1+
items.maps_to: `guide/topics/manifest/service-element` (`isolatedProcess`); AOSP security-model paper Table 2 (Android 4.1): "Isolated process: Apps may run services in a process with no Android permissions and access to only two binder services. For example, the Chrome browser runs its renderer in an isolated process", mitigating [T.A3][T.A2][T.A5][T.A6][T.A7]; SELinux `isolated_app` domain
items.test:
`android:isolatedProcess="true"` is the correct container for parsing untrusted input (media,
archives, native decoders): the process has no permissions of its own and access to only two binder
services. Its **absence** around a native parser is the finding; its **presence** is not a bypassable
control, and claiming otherwise gets a report rejected.
D03-038 (global `android:process` / missing `isolatedProcess`) points here for the `ps -AZ` proof; the
external-service direction is D06-087.
items.how:
```bash
grep -nE 'isolatedProcess|externalService' $DEC/apktool/AndroidManifest.xml
grep -rnE 'MediaCodec|ImageDecoder|BitmapFactory|ZipInputStream|System\.loadLibrary' $DEC/jadx/sources/
adb shell ps -AZ | grep -E 'isolated_app|com.target.app'
```
items.proof:
`ps -AZ` showing the parsing work in `u:r:untrusted_app:s0` (one process, full app
permissions) rather than `u:r:isolated_app:s0:c…`, while the app ingests attacker-supplied files. Verify
with `ps -AZ`, not with the manifest alone.
items.escalation:
This is the honest **downgrade** for a memory-corruption finding in a parser that runs
isolated, and the honest **upgrade** argument when the same parser runs in the app domain — a
main-process parser bug is app compromise. → D16.
items.ruled_out_when:
`ps -AZ` shows the parser in `isolated_app` while it handles the untrusted input —
record the SELinux context string in the ruled-out register.

items.title: Binder domains and vendor interfaces are not app-reachable — the false-positive gate
items.severity_note: Support — Medium as an OEM-VRP report for the `@VintfStability` variant
items.vrt: n/a — this gate stops an over-rated report
items.applies_to: Android 8+ (multiple binder contexts, introduced with Treble); the AIDL-HAL variant is Android 11+ and OEM/vendor images only
items.maps_to: AOSP "Binder IPC": `/dev/binder` = framework/app AIDL, `/dev/hwbinder` = framework↔vendor and vendor↔vendor HIDL, `/dev/vndbinder` = vendor↔vendor AIDL with its own `vndservicemanager`; contexts are isolated so "binder nodes passed through a specific context are accessible only within that same context"; `ProcessState::initWithDriver("/dev/vndbinder")`. AOSP "AIDL for HALs": `@VintfStability` + `stability: "vintf"`; `vts_treble_vintf_vendor_test` verifies frozen interfaces "are frozen at a known released version… both sides of the interface agree on the exact definition".
items.test:
Apps talk on `/dev/binder` **only**. A "vulnerability" in a HIDL or vendor-AIDL HAL is an
app-level finding only if there is a framework service on `/dev/binder` that proxies to it — prove the
proxy path before rating anything. The related OEM case: a `@VintfStability` interface shipped unfrozen
or locally modified is a version-mismatch surface, but it is not an app finding unless you can drive it
from an app.
items.how:
```bash
adb shell ls -lZ /dev/binder /dev/hwbinder /dev/vndbinder
adb shell lshal 2>/dev/null | head                 # hwbinder registrations
adb shell service list | grep -i <hal-name>        # is there an app-reachable framework proxy?
adb shell dmesg | grep -i 'avc.*vndbinder'
adb shell cat /vendor/etc/vintf/manifest.xml | grep -A4 '<hal format="aidl"'
```
The shared probe's `bind` step (`--ez dump true` sends `DUMP_TRANSACTION` with the reader thread started first) is the AM-03 vehicle — D06-082.
items.proof:
A framework service name in `service list` for which `getService()` returns non-null from the
app's UID, and whose decompiled code forwards to the vendor HAL. Absent that, record the surface as
**not app-reachable** in the ruled-out register. For the OEM variant: a `<version>` in the device
manifest that does not exist in AOSP's frozen API directory for that interface, or a
`vts_treble_vintf_vendor_test` failure.
items.escalation:
→ D25 when a proxy exists; → D17 for the parcel-mismatch consequence of a drifted
interface.
items.ruled_out_when:
`service list` contains no framework proxy for the HAL, or `getService()` returns
null from an app UID — this is the mechanism, and it is the whole point of the item.

items.title: Binder threadpool re-entrancy — check-then-act races, proved statistically
items.vrt: `broken_access_control.privilege_escalation` (varies); `broken_access_control.idor.modify_sensitive_information_iterable_object_identifiers` (P2) when the race duplicates a ledger entry
items.applies_to: All
items.maps_to: `guide/components/processes-and-threads` — "`IBinder` methods execute in a thread pool, not the UI thread"; ContentProvider `query/insert/delete/update/getType` "are called from a pool of threads… must be implemented as thread-safe"; AOSP "Binder threading" (per-process shared threadpool, reentrancy on the same binder thread for nested calls)
items.test:
Incoming binder calls are dispatched on a pool of threads. Any service that validates and then
acts on shared mutable state without synchronisation is racey from a remote attacker who simply calls
concurrently — a double-redeem, double-spend or duplicate-grant.
items.how:
```bash
grep -rnE 'class .*\$Stub|public .* onTransact' $DEC/jadx/sources/ -A5 | grep -vE 'synchronized|AtomicReference|ReentrantLock|Mutex'
```
```java
ExecutorService ex = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(32);
for (int i = 0; i < 5000; i++) { final int k = i; ex.submit(() -> svc.redeem(k % 2 == 0 ? "valid" : "other")); }
```
items.proof:
**A distribution, not an outlier.** Run at least 10 interleaved trials per group (control and
test, randomised order, not back-to-back) and report mean, median and σ per group; a signal requires the
suspect group's mean to sit ≥ 2σ from the control's. For a redeem race the cleaner proof is the ledger:
the count of granted entitlements exceeding the intended single grant, shown in the app's own database
or in the backend response. One lucky double-grant is not a finding.
items.escalation: → D23 (entitlement or payment fraud), → D15 (the backend race the service exposes).
items.ruled_out_when:
The check-then-act region is `synchronized` (or uses an atomic compare-and-set, or a
database unique constraint), and 100+ concurrent attempts produce exactly one grant — state the attempt
count in the ruled-out register.

items.title: Local socket or localhost HTTP server bound by the app without authentication
items.vrt: `sensitive_data_exposure.disclosure_of_secrets.for_publicly_accessible_asset` (P1) when bound to `0.0.0.0` and serving data or commands to the LAN; `broken_access_control.privilege_escalation` (varies) for localhost-only
items.attacker: AM-03 for localhost; **AM-06** for a `0.0.0.0` bind
items.applies_to: All. Frequently a leftover from React Native / Flutter debug tooling — cross-check D19.
items.maps_to: MASWE-0018 mode "Binding a local web service or open port that accepts connections without authentication" (CWE-306, CWE-749); MASTG-TECH-0028 (Get Open Connections); MASVS-PLATFORM-1; Mobile Top 10 2024 M3/M8
items.test:
Debug bridges, RN dev servers, WebView-backing local servers and SDK IPC channels all bind
sockets. Any app on the device — and, when bound to `0.0.0.0`, anything on the LAN — can reach them.
items.how:
```bash
adb shell "cat /proc/net/tcp /proc/net/tcp6 /proc/net/unix" | head -60
adb shell netstat -lntp 2>/dev/null || adb shell cat /proc/net/tcp /proc/net/tcp6   # toybox has no ss
adb shell ps -A -o PID,UID,NAME | grep com.target.app          # map the socket to the app's UID
adb forward tcp:18080 tcp:<port> && curl -s -i http://127.0.0.1:18080/   # host curl through adb forward (the device has no curl); then re-prove from the probe — a different UID on-device
adb shell "echo hello | nc 127.0.0.1 <port>"
grep -rnE 'new ServerSocket\(|LocalServerSocket\(|NanoHTTPD|ktor|embeddedServer|0\.0\.0\.0' $DEC/jadx/sources/
```
items.proof:
A response from the port obtained by a process running as a different UID, returning app data
or accepting a state-changing command. A bind to `0.0.0.0` rather than `127.0.0.1` widens this to the
whole LAN — capture `nc -v <device-ip> <port>` from a second host as the evidence.
items.escalation:
A localhost server reachable from a WebView (D10) is scriptable by any page the WebView
loads, converting it into a remote primitive.
items.ruled_out_when:
`/proc/net/tcp` shows the listener bound to `0100007F` (127.0.0.1) **and** every
request requires a token the app generated at runtime and never wrote to a world-readable location —
prove by connecting without the token and getting a rejection whose body differs from the success body.

items.title: Shell-backed binder brokers (Shizuku-class) as an assumed-privilege path
items.severity_note: High — as a fleet/MDM finding; as an app finding, only when the app itself exposes such a broker or trusts state a broker can forge
items.vrt: `broken_access_control.privilege_escalation` (varies)
items.attacker: AM-04 (the user completes the pairing flow)
items.applies_to: Android 11+ (wireless debugging pairing). Boundaries still apply: shell cannot read `/data/user/0/<pkg>`, and shell permissions are trimmed by release and by OEM.
items.maps_to: HackTricks `shizuku-privileged-api.md`; ATT&CK T1626 (Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism)
items.test:
Whether the target app, or any app on a managed fleet, brokers privileged binder calls through
an ADB/shell-backed service. That is ADB-equivalent privilege with no root and no USB cable.
items.how:
```bash
adb shell service list | grep -i shizuku
adb shell dumpsys activity service moe.shizuku.privileged.api | head
# from the broker shell
./rish ; id            # uid=2000(shell) … context=u:r:shell:s0
cmd appops set com.target.app SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW allow
cmd connectivity set-package-networking-enabled false com.example.agent
```
items.proof:
A shell-UID binder helper spawned from an app workflow; `Shizuku.getUid()` returning `2000`
(shell backend) or `0` (root backend); AppOps or per-package networking changed from inside an app
process.
items.escalation:
The malicious variant chains Accessibility → Settings → enable wireless debugging →
scrape the pairing code from the UI tree → pair to `127.0.0.1` → spawn a UID-2000 helper over binder.
Detection signals worth reporting to a fleet owner: accessibility-driven taps on "Build number", an
`APPLICATION_DEVELOPMENT_SETTINGS` launch, local ADB TLS/SPAKE2 to `127.0.0.1`, silent
`WRITE_SECURE_SETTINGS` grants, and `BOOT_COMPLETED` receivers restoring debugging state.
items.ruled_out_when:
The app neither exposes such a broker nor makes a trust decision on any state a
shell-UID process can set (AppOps, secure settings, package-networking state) — name the decisions you
checked.

items.title: Service acting as a network proxy or registering a `VpnService`
items.vrt: `broken_access_control.privilege_escalation` (varies); `sensitive_data_exposure.disclosure_of_secrets.pii_leakage_exposure` (varies) for the redirected traffic
items.attacker: AM-06 for a LAN-reachable listener; AM-09 for the VPN case
items.applies_to: All
items.maps_to: ATT&CK T1604 (Proxy Through Victim — "On Android specifically, attackers can use the `Proxy` API to establish SOCKS proxy connections or interact with raw sockets directly"; Exobot S0522 "can open a SOCKS proxy connection through the compromised device"); T1638 (Adversary-in-the-Middle — "a malicious application may register itself as a VPN client, effectively redirecting device traffic to adversary-owned resources"); T1428 (Exploitation of Remote Services); DressCode S0300 "general purpose tunnel"; mitigation M1012
items.test:
Does the app open a listening socket, relay traffic, or register a `VpnService`? Either turns
the user's device — its IP, and its LAN position — into infrastructure for someone else.
items.how:
```bash
grep -rnE 'ServerSocket|VpnService|Proxy\(|SOCKS|java\.net\.Proxy|LocalServerSocket|accept\(' $DEC/jadx/sources/
aapt2 dump permissions apk/base.apk | grep -E 'BIND_VPN_SERVICE|INTERNET'
adb shell "cat /proc/net/tcp /proc/net/tcp6" | awk '{print $2,$4,$8}' | sort -u
adb shell dumpsys connectivity | grep -i vpn
```
items.proof:
A LISTEN socket owned by the app's UID reachable from another host on the same network
(`nc -v <device-ip> <port>` succeeding), or the VPN key icon active with the app named in
`dumpsys connectivity`.
items.escalation:
A listening socket on a corporate-managed handset is a lateral-movement foothold; the
mitigation to recommend is M1012 per-app VPN. Traffic attribution and abuse takedowns are the business
impact to state.
items.ruled_out_when:
No socket is in LISTEN state on a non-loopback address for the app's UID, and no
`VpnService` is declared — attach the `/proc/net/tcp` capture as the negative's evidence.

items.title: Remote-support / screen-share module embedded as a service
items.vrt: `broken_authentication_and_session_management.authentication_bypass` (P1) when a session can be started or joined without per-session user consent
items.attacker: AM-01 / AM-02 depending on how a session is initiated
items.applies_to: All. `MediaProjection` requires a user-consent dialog per session — verify the app does not cache or reuse the projection token beyond its session.
items.maps_to: ATT&CK T1663 (Remote Access Software — names "VNC, TeamViewer, AirDroid, AirMirror" and notes such software "typically requires many privileged permissions, such as accessibility services or device administrator"), T1513 (Screen Capture), T1516 (Input Injection); mitigation M1012
items.test:
Does the app embed screen-sharing or remote-control functionality — a VNC/agent SDK, a support
module that streams the screen or accepts remote input? These need the highest-risk permissions on the
platform, and the interesting question is the **authorisation of the session**, not its existence.
items.how:
```bash
grep -rn -iE 'vnc|rfb|teamviewer|airdroid|airmirror|cobrowse|screenshare|remote.?control|MediaProjection|dispatchGesture|injectInputEvent' $DEC/jadx/sources/
aapt2 dump permissions apk/base.apk | grep -E 'BIND_ACCESSIBILITY_SERVICE|SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW|FOREGROUND_SERVICE_MEDIA_PROJECTION'
adb shell dumpsys media_projection
```
items.proof:
A running session in which the remote side both sees the screen and injects a tap — record
both ends. Then test the authorisation: can a session be initiated or joined without explicit
per-session user consent (a guessable session code, a server-initiated start, a reused projection
token)?
items.escalation:
Remote view plus remote input equals full in-app account takeover with the user's own
device doing the work; rate on the most sensitive action reachable in-session.
items.ruled_out_when:
Every session requires a fresh, user-visible consent (the `MediaProjection` dialog
plus an in-app confirmation) and the session code has adequate entropy — measure it, do not eyeball it.

items.title: Cast / remote-playback session as an unauthenticated control and content channel
items.vrt: `sensitive_data_exposure.disclosure_of_secrets.for_publicly_accessible_asset` (P1) when the cast payload carries a reusable account token; `broken_access_control.privilege_escalation` (varies) for a signed-URL entitlement bypass
items.applies_to: Apps integrating the Google Cast SDK or remote playback
items.maps_to: No external identifier verified in this session — cite the captured traffic, not a standard.
items.test:
Cast-enabled apps hand a receiver device a media URL and, frequently, an auth token or signed
URL in `MediaInfo` custom data. Two questions: does that payload carry a bearer token or long-lived
signed URL to a device on the LAN in the clear, and can a same-network party enumerate or hijack the
session?
items.how:
```bash
grep -rnE 'CastContext|SessionManager|RemoteMediaClient|MediaInfo\.Builder|setCustomData|CastOptions|setReceiverApplicationId' $DEC/jadx/sources/
tcpdump -i any -s0 -w cast.pcap 'port 8008 or port 8009 or port 5353'
tshark -r cast.pcap -Y 'mdns || tcp.port==8009' -T fields -e _ws.col.Info
```
items.proof:
The captured payload (or a `RemoteMediaClient` log) containing a bearer token or signed URL
that **still authenticates when replayed with `curl` from off-device** — that replay is the finding, not
the capture.
items.escalation:
A token on the LAN is a full D13 session-theft primitive; a long-TTL signed URL is a D23
entitlement bypass.
items.ruled_out_when:
The cast payload carries only short-lived, single-use, device-bound URLs — replay
one from another host and show it rejected.

items.title: THE LAYER-ORDERING TRAP, binder edition — an argument error does not prove you passed the caller check
items.severity_note: Support — a kill gate on every authorisation-bypass claim in this domain
items.vrt: n/a
items.applies_to: **Every** auth-bypass claim in this chapter, and every APK-derived HTTP endpoint the service calls
items.maps_to: `triage-validation` "THE LAYER-ORDERING TRAP"; CVE-2026-0047 ("Phase 1: Confirming the Bug") for the binder-side oracle
items.test:
The single highest-confidence false positive in the whole auth-bypass class. On the wire, many
stacks run a body parser or sanitiser **in front of** the auth middleware, so a malformed body is
rejected before auth is ever consulted and the response is indistinguishable from "auth passed,
validation failed". The binder analogue is exact: `Stub.onTransact` unmarshals every argument from the
`Parcel` **before** dispatching to your method, so a `BadParcelableException`, `IllegalArgumentException`
or `NullPointerException` raised in `onTransact` itself tells you only that your parcel was malformed —
the permission check may sit immediately after, untouched.
items.how:
Re-test with a **minimal well-formed** call. On the binder side, read the frame the exception
came from:
```bash
adb shell service call <svc> <code>            # garbage args
# inspect the Parcel's stack trace: which frame raised?
#   ...at IFoo$Stub.onTransact(IFoo.java:NNN)      -> unmarshalling, proves nothing
#   ...at FooService.doThing(FooService.java:NNN)  -> METHOD BODY EXECUTED, no check ran
```
The HTTP side of whatever the service calls is D01-078 (the canonical layer-ordering item) — run it there.
items.proof:
The *frame* the exception was raised in, not the exception class. An error naming **input
shape or character class** means you are talking to a parser; an error naming a **domain field**, with a
well-formed minimal body, is real signal.
items.escalation: n/a — this is a kill gate. It prevents a false Critical against a production service.
items.ruled_out_when:
The exception frame is inside the service method (or the well-formed `{}` still
returns the domain error) — then the bypass claim stands and you proceed.

items.title: Shadow API — the bound service is a bridge to an older backend version

items.applies_to: Any versioned API — and the app's hardcoded calls are the number-one source of old-version endpoints
items.maps_to: `hunt-shadow-api` Stages 1 & 3 and its severity table
items.test:
Pointer — the shadow-API diff is owned by D15-012 (and D05-060 for the broadcast-harvested route
inventory): the bound service's hardcoded endpoint set is its input. Extract it here into
`recon/app-endpoints.txt` and run the four-axis diff (auth strength, rate limiting, input validation, field
exposure) there. **The bug is the delta, not the version.**

```bash
grep -rnE 'https?://[A-Za-z0-9.-]+/[A-Za-z0-9/._-]*' "$DEC/jadx/sources" | grep -oE 'https?://[^"'"'"']+' | sort -u > recon/app-endpoints.txt
python3 scripts/item.py D15-012
```
items.proof: As D15-012 — a security regression on the old path, demonstrated with the same request against both versions; recorded under D15-012.

items.ruled_out_when: n/a — recorded under D15-012; this row carries only the endpoint-extraction deliverable (`recon/app-endpoints.txt` present and non-empty, or empty with the grep quoted).

items.title: Confirm the SELinux domain before claiming an escalation `untrusted_app` cannot perform
items.vrt: n/a
items.applies_to: Android 5.x+ (SELinux enforcing for all userspace); Android 9+ for the per-app SELinux sandbox at targetSdk ≥ 28
items.maps_to: source.android.com SELinux concepts (contexts, `permissive=0` meaning enforcing) and device-policy (the note that excluding `untrusted_app` from a rule is "trivial to work around because all apps may optionally run services in the `isolated_app` domain" — which cuts both ways, since `isolated_app` is strictly weaker)
items.test:
Before writing "the attacker then gains root" or "then reads another app's data directory",
confirm the SELinux policy permits it. Per-app MLS categories mean app A's `c168,…` cannot touch app B's
files, and no amount of binder access changes that.
items.how:
```bash
adb shell ps -Z | grep com.poc.attacker        # expect u:r:untrusted_app:s0:c…,c…
adb shell dmesg | grep 'avc: '                 # what actually got denied during the PoC
adb logcat -b all | grep 'avc: '
```
items.proof:
An AVC line of the documented shape —
`avc: denied { read write } for pid=8821 comm="poc" scontext=u:r:untrusted_app:s0 tcontext=… tclass=file permissive=0`
— proving the step you were about to claim did not happen. Conversely, the **absence** of an AVC denial
plus successful data return proves the step did.
items.escalation:
None — it prunes invalid chains before they reach the report, which is the highest-value
thing this item does.
items.ruled_out_when:
The claimed step produced no AVC denial and returned the data, recorded with the
`dmesg` capture taken during the PoC run.

items.title: Marker discipline and the body-diff rule for binder returns
items.vrt: n/a
items.applies_to: Every "the service returned my data" and "the service consumed my input" claim
items.maps_to: `bb-methodology` PART 4 (Marker Discipline, Body-Diff Rule)
items.test:
Shared doctrine with D05-010, D07-050, D08-063 and D13-003 (marker discipline); the binder-specific additions are the two failure modes below and the `xxd` byte-diff of returned Parcels. Two failure modes specific to this domain. (a) **Reflection false positives:** you put a value
in a `Bundle`, see it in a log line, and conclude the service consumed it — when the string was already
there. (b) **Non-differential returns:** you get a populated `Bundle` back from an unprivileged bind and
call it a leak, when a caller with no permission could obtain the same content from a public API.
items.how:
Use a random alphanumeric marker of **8+ characters** with no English words and no protocol
keywords — never `test`, `marker`, `evil`, `attacker`, `payload`, `AAAA`, or your own domain. Good:
`cpmark987abc`, `x4hd2k9pq`. **Search the baseline for the marker before claiming anything:**
```bash
adb logcat -c
adb shell am startservice -n com.target.app/.SyncService --es note "x4hd2k9pq"
adb logcat -d > with-marker.txt
adb logcat -c && adb shell am startservice -n com.target.app/.SyncService && adb logcat -d > baseline.txt
grep -c 'x4hd2k9pq' baseline.txt      # MUST be 0
diff baseline.txt with-marker.txt
```
For returns, diff the bytes:
```bash
diff <(xxd unprivileged-return.bin) <(xxd legitimate-return.bin)
```
items.proof:
The marker present in the test artefact and **absent from the baseline**; and, for a
disclosure claim, a byte-level diff showing the unprivileged return contains content the legitimate
low-privilege path does not. A byte-identical return is not a leak.
items.escalation: n/a — it protects every other item's evidence.
items.ruled_out_when:
The marker appears in the baseline (word collision — the claim dies), or the
privileged and unprivileged returns are byte-identical.

items.title: Evidence hygiene for a service-driven state change
items.vrt: n/a
items.applies_to: Every state-change finding in this chapter (credential overwrite, entitlement flip, service stop, file drop)
items.maps_to: `evidence-hygiene` §§2, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8
items.test:
Shared doctrine with D04-065, D11-071 and D13-008 (the five-shot pattern); the binder-specific addition is capturing the probe's `dumpsys package` requested-permission block beside every step. A state change needs pre-state, the bug, and post-state — plus the out-of-band side effect.
Five artefacts, taken in one sitting, filenames `{finding-#}-step{n}-{description}.png`:
(1) pre-state verification (the old PIN still works; the file is absent; the service is running);
(2) **the bug itself** — the binder call succeeding from the zero-permission PoC, with the PoC's
manifest visible; (3) post-state negative (the old value no longer works); (4) post-state positive (the
attacker's value works); (5) the side effect (the request at your collaborator, the file in the victim's
directory, the inbox).
items.how:
Capture the PoC app's identity alongside every step:
```bash
adb shell dumpsys package com.poc.attacker | sed -n '/requested permissions/,/install permissions/p'
adb shell dumpsys package com.poc.attacker | grep -E 'userId=|pkgFlags'
adb logcat -c && <run the PoC> && adb logcat -d > evidence/04-step2-binder-call.txt
```
Sanitise transcripts, keeping what triage needs:
```bash
sed -E 's/(Bearer )[A-Za-z0-9._-]{20,}/\1<REDACTED>/g; s/("token":")[^"]+/\1<REDACTED>/g' raw.txt > evidence/raw.sanitised.txt
grep -iE 'authorization|"token"|set-cookie' evidence/raw.sanitised.txt | head   # verify
```
**Leave visible:** trace ids (`x-request-id`, `x-datadog-trace-id`), your own attacker UID and package
name, JSON key names, transaction codes, method names. **Mask:** token and cookie *values*, the victim
account's PII. Keep the unredacted originals locally for triager verification through the platform's
private attachment system — never email.
items.proof: Five numbered, cross-referenced artefacts plus the PoC app's manifest in the evidence tree.
items.escalation: n/a.
items.ruled_out_when: n/a — this is a deliverable standard, not a test.

items.title: `adb shell` is UID 2000 — re-prove every candidate from a zero-permission app
items.severity_note: Support — governs the attacker model of every finding in this chapter
items.vrt: n/a
items.attacker: Decides whether you may write AM-03 at all
items.applies_to: Every dynamic test in this chapter
items.maps_to: `docs/05-attacker-models.md` (AM-03: "Your PoC for this model is a **second app**, not an adb command"); ISSUES.md Phase 5 exit condition
items.test:
Shared doctrine with D04-005 and D05-011 (one re-proof rule per component chapter); the binder-specific part is the UID check and the probe launch below. `adb shell am startservice`, `service call` and drozer run as UID 2000 (`shell`) on a stock device
and as **UID 0 after `adb root` or on a rooted AVD** — root reaches `exported=false` components outright, so an
AVD reachability result is a root artefact until re-proved from the probe; `shell` itself holds far more
privilege than any real attacker, including, on many builds, permissions no third-party app can obtain.
Check `adb shell id` and record it in the log header. Discovery with adb is fine and fast. **A finding proved only by adb has not established
AM-03**, and a triager who notices will downgrade the whole report.
items.how:
The shared probe (D06-082) is that app, already built — use its `bind`/`start`/`getservice` steps
before writing a client. Where a custom client is unavoidable, build one PoC app whose manifest declares **no** `<uses-permission>` at all, signed
with a throwaway key, containing the regenerated `.aidl` (same package and interface name as the target)
and a `bindService` call per candidate. Add a `<queries>` entry for the target package when your PoC
targets SDK 30+ — that is a one-line manifest addition, not a mitigation.
```xml
<manifest package="com.poc.attacker">
  <queries><package android:name="com.target.app" /></queries>
  <application android:label="poc"><activity android:name=".Main" android:exported="true"/></application>
</manifest>
```
```bash
adb install -r poc.apk
adb shell dumpsys package com.poc.attacker | sed -n '/requested permissions/,/User 0/p'   # must be empty
adb shell id   # uid=2000 (stock) or uid=0 (rooted AVD) — record it
adb shell am start -S -n com.poc.attacker/.Main -f 0x10008000   # -S kills the stale task; the flag forces a fresh task instead of delivering to a task whose top is the victim
```
items.proof:
The `dumpsys` output showing an empty requested-permission list, the PoC's manifest in the
evidence tree, and the privileged result in the PoC's own logcat tag — not in `adb shell` output.
items.escalation: n/a — it sets the precondition sentence, which is worth several rating steps.
items.ruled_out_when:
The candidate reproduces from adb but **not** from the PoC app. That is a real
negative and must be recorded as one, naming the permission or platform gate that `shell` held and the
app did not.

items.title: Severity governance and chain-filing order for binder findings
items.vrt: n/a — governs the VRT choice for every other item
items.applies_to: Every Critical or High claim arising from this chapter
items.maps_to: `triage-validation` PRE-SEVERITY GATE; `bugcrowd-reporting` §§1–3, 5
items.test:
Run the pre-severity gate against the **Critical claim**, not against the bug. Substitute the
claim into each question: (1) Have I validated the full chain to attacker-attainable impact, or only one
primitive in the middle — "unauthenticated binder method confirmed" is not "account takeover"? (2) What
does the attacker walk away with, in one concrete sentence? (3) Have I personally reproduced the full
chain end to end **at least twice**? (4) Is there still an inheritance gate, signature check or audience
check gating the chain — if yes it is not Critical, it is "primitive present" at a lower severity?
(5) Has the programme rejected this severity class before?
items.how:
File in this order, because a consumer report must reference primitive ids that already exist:
1. Identify the highest-severity chained outcome.
2. File each primitive separately at its standalone severity — the unauthenticated interface (D06-015),
   the path-traversal write (D06-030), the token disclosure (D06-028) — leaving a placeholder
   cross-reference line.
3. File the chain consumer with the full ATO/RCE narrative at the chained severity, filling in the real
   primitive ids.
4. Edit each primitive to backfill the consumer's id.
Consumer body:
```markdown
**Chain partners (filed as separate reports)**
- submission [UUID-1] — unauthenticated AIDL interface on com.target.app/.SyncService
- submission [UUID-2] — caller-controlled savePath in tryDownload()
These primitives have independent fix surfaces and are filed separately per the programme's
"one fix = one bounty" rule.
```
(The template is a report-body paragraph, not a markdown heading — a `## ` line inside this fence is read
by the chapter grammar as a section break and strands the fields below it.)
Pick the most **specific accurate** VRT node and then set technical severity manually; never pick a node
that misrepresents the bug to get a higher default. Open the body with the literal heading
`## Severity request — please review carefully before applying VRT default` and anchor the argument in
the CVSS vector plus the programme's own focus-area wording.
items.proof:
Cross-referenced ids in both directions, and a severity-request paragraph as the first body
section.
items.escalation:
A chain is a **severity amplifier, not a merge request**. Do not paste the whole chain
narrative into every primitive, do not claim each primitive is independently P1, and do not file
everything within minutes of each other — triagers read that as spam.
items.ruled_out_when:
n/a. One caveat that is not a rule but its inverse: **do not retract a confirmed
finding that stopped reproducing because the client patched mid-engagement.** Keep the timestamped
pre-patch request/response; the difference between a retraction and a preserved Critical is whether you
have that evidence.

items.title: Drive every binder candidate through the shared probe's `bind` / `start` / `getservice` steps — never a per-target client
items.vrt: n/a — method
items.applies_to: All
items.maps_to: docs/05 (AM-03: the PoC is a second app, not an adb command); attacker-app/README.md (`bind`, `start`, `getservice` steps)
items.record: logs/D06-082.txt (index: component → steps run → verdict counts); logs/D06-082-<component>.txt (raw `PROBE|` lines per component); pocs/F-NNN/ once a step returns data
items.skip_when: `inventory/components.csv` has no `type=service` row with `exported=true` and probe 3 of the applicability probe is 0 — write `n/a — D06-082: no exported service and no client-side bind to drive`.
items.test:
The probe is the AM-03 vehicle. Its `bind` step binds an explicit component, calls
`getInterfaceDescriptor()`, then sweeps the transaction codes in `--es codes lo-hi` with
`data.writeInterfaceToken(descriptor)` and classifies each reply by exception frame (D06-075); `--ez callback true`
hands the service a Binder of ours (`PROBE|bind|callback_transact=…`) and `--ez dump true` sends
`DUMP_TRANSACTION` through a pipe with the reader thread started first (D06-014). `start` delivers an explicit
`startService`/`startForegroundService` with typed extras; `getservice` reflects `ServiceManager.getService(name)`
and reports null/non-null for the app UID.
items.how:
```bash
adb shell "am start -S -n com.sanehunters.probe/.MainActivity --es run bind --es victim com.target.app --es component .ExportedService --es codes 1-64 --ez callback true --ez dump true"
```

items.title: Verified-caller cache keyed on package name — the signature check runs once, the name check runs forever
items.vrt: `broken_access_control.privilege_escalation` (varies); `broken_authentication_and_session_management.authentication_bypass` (P1) when the impersonated peer's methods mint auth material
items.applies_to: All apps whose caller check resolves a UID to a package name and memoises the result
items.maps_to: MASWE-0018 (CWE-926); `developer.android.com/reference/android/content/pm/PackageManager` (`hasSigningCertificate`, `checkSignatures` — a sideloaded package can carry any package name)
items.record: logs/D06-083.txt (the Frida trace of the verifier per caller); pocs/F-NNN/ with the same-name stub's manifest and signing key fingerprint
items.skip_when: `grep -rlE 'hasSigningCertificate|checkSignatures|GET_SIGNING_CERTIFICATES' $DEC/jadx/sources | wc -l` prints 0 — write `n/a — D06-083: no signature check exists to be cached (D06-020 governs)`.
items.test:
Verifiers often memoise the result of a signature check in a field keyed on the package name
(`lastVerifiedPkg`, a `Set<String>`, an LRU). The cache is sound only if the write is gated by the signature
check **and** the key includes the UID or the certificate hash. A cache keyed on name alone, written on first
contact, lets a later caller with the same name (a sideloaded stub installed after the real peer is removed, or
a shared-UID sibling) pass on the name match.
items.how:
```bash
grep -rnE 'hasSigningCertificate|checkSignatures|GET_SIGNING_CERTIFICATES' "$DEC/jadx/sources" -B15 -A15 | grep -nE 'this\.[A-Za-z_]+ = |\.put\(|\.add\(|\.contains\(|\.containsKey\(|\.get\('
# per hit: what is the cache key (name, uid, cert hash)? is the write inside the branch where the signature matched? is it ever cleared on package change?
```
Runtime: hook the verifier, call once from the real peer (or let the app do so), uninstall the peer, install a
same-name stub signed with a throwaway key, call again and log whether the signature path ran.
items.proof:
The decompiled cache write with its key, plus a Frida trace showing the signature method called for
the first caller and not for the same-name stub, plus the stub receiving the privileged return.
items.escalation: Same as D06-020 — the attacker is the vendor's companion app for every method on the interface.
items.ruled_out_when:
The cache key includes the calling UID or the certificate digest, the write is lexically
inside the signature-match branch, and a `PACKAGE_REPLACED`/`PACKAGE_REMOVED` receiver or a per-process lifetime
clears it — show the key and the write site.

items.title: Proxy service delivers permission-gated data without `checkPermissionForDataDelivery` on the caller's `AttributionSource`
items.vrt: `broken_access_control.privilege_escalation` (varies) — a runtime-permission bypass; `sensitive_data_exposure.disclosure_of_secrets.pii_leakage_exposure` (varies) on the data
items.applies_to: API 31+ (`AttributionSource`); any service whose method returns data that a runtime permission guards
items.maps_to: `developer.android.com/about/versions/12/behavior-changes-12` (attribution / data-delivery permission checks); `developer.android.com/reference/androidx/core/content/PermissionChecker` (`checkPermissionForDataDelivery`, `checkCallingOrSelfPermissionForDataDelivery`); `android.content.AttributionSource` (`enforceCallingUid`); MASWE-0018
items.record: logs/D06-085.txt (the probe's returned data head and the `appops get` block); screenshots/D06-085-1.png (the privacy indicator / app-op history blaming the victim)
items.skip_when: `grep -rlE 'LocationManager|FusedLocationProviderClient|AudioRecord|MediaRecorder|ContactsContract|CallLog|Telephony\.Sms|BluetoothLeScanner' $DEC/jadx/sources | xargs grep -lE 'Stub|onBind|handleMessage' | wc -l` prints 0 — write `n/a — D06-085: no binder-exposed class touches a runtime-permission-gated resource`.
items.test:
From Android 12 a component that accesses a permission-gated resource **for another app** must pass
the caller's `AttributionSource` (built with `Context.createAttributionContext` or received over the binder and
verified with `enforceCallingUid()`) and check it with
`PermissionChecker.checkPermissionForDataDelivery(context, perm, pid, uid, packageName, attributionTag, message)`,
which also notes the app-op against the caller. `checkSelfPermission` or `checkCallingOrSelfPermission` passes
whenever the *app* holds the permission, so a caller without it receives the data and the privacy indicator /
app-op history blame the victim.
items.how:
```bash
grep -rlE 'LocationManager|FusedLocationProviderClient|AudioRecord|MediaRecorder|ContactsContract|CallLog|Telephony\.Sms|getDeviceId|BluetoothLeScanner' "$DEC/jadx/sources" | xargs grep -lE 'Stub|onBind|handleMessage' > "$E/recon/D06-085-proxy-candidates.txt"
xargs grep -nE 'checkPermissionForDataDelivery|checkCallingOrSelfPermissionForDataDelivery|AttributionSource|enforceCallingUid|checkSelfPermission|checkCallingOrSelfPermission' < "$E/recon/D06-085-proxy-candidates.txt"
adb shell appops get com.target.app | grep -iE 'COARSE_LOCATION|FINE_LOCATION|RECORD_AUDIO|READ_CONTACTS'   # whose op gets noted when the probe calls?
```
items.proof:
The probe (no `<uses-permission>`) receiving a location fix / audio bytes / contact rows from the
method, plus `appops get` or `dumpsys appops` showing the access noted against the victim package only, plus
the decompiled check being `checkSelfPermission`/`checkCallingOrSelfPermission`.
items.escalation:
→ D20 (silent sensor access under the victim's grant); pair with D06-035/040 when the proxy also
starts a sensor FGS.
items.ruled_out_when:
Every proxied access runs `checkPermissionForDataDelivery` (or the `ForDataDelivery` family)
against a caller-derived `AttributionSource` that was `enforceCallingUid()`-verified, and the probe gets
`SecurityException`/`PERMISSION_DENIED` — name the method and the line.

items.title: Send `DUMP_TRANSACTION` / `SHELL_COMMAND_TRANSACTION` to every bound IBinder — an overridden `dump()` has no caller check
items.vrt: `sensitive_data_exposure.disclosure_of_secrets.for_publicly_accessible_asset` (P1) when the dump prints a live token; `sensitive_data_exposure.disclosure_of_secrets.pii_leakage_exposure` (varies) otherwise
items.applies_to: All exported bound services
items.maps_to: `android.os.IBinder` (`DUMP_TRANSACTION`, `SHELL_COMMAND_TRANSACTION`, `INTERFACE_TRANSACTION`, `PING_TRANSACTION`); `android.os.Binder.dump(FileDescriptor, String[])` / `onShellCommand` (no permission enforced by the base class); CWE-280

items.test:
`Binder.execTransact` routes the reserved codes to `dump()`, `shellCommand()` and
`getInterfaceDescriptor()` before `onTransact`. The base implementations are empty; a service that overrides
`dump(FileDescriptor, PrintWriter, String[])` (for `dumpsys activity service`) or `onShellCommand` answers
**any** holder of the binder.
items.proof:
Non-zero bytes from the probe (empty manifest permissions) containing state the caller could not
otherwise read; the overriding `dump` body quoted by `file:line`.
items.escalation: A token in the dump → D13/D15; a writable path or queue entry → D06-030.
items.ruled_out_when:
No app class overrides `dump`/`onShellCommand` on a binder that an exported service returns,
or the override starts with a caller check — and the probe's `dump` step returns 0 bytes for every bound service.

items.title: `externalService` bound with `BIND_EXTERNAL_SERVICE` — foreign code running as the app's UID
items.vrt: `broken_access_control.privilege_escalation` (varies)
items.attacker: AM-08 (the SDK/peer whose service is bound); AM-03 when the app's own external service is exported
items.applies_to: API 24+ (`android:externalService`, `Context.BIND_EXTERNAL_SERVICE`)
items.maps_to: `developer.android.com/reference/android/content/Context#BIND_EXTERNAL_SERVICE` ("the service will run in the client's package and UID … must be isolatedProcess and exported"); `developer.android.com/reference/android/R.attr#externalService`; MASWE-0018

items.test:
Two directions. (a) The app calls `bindService(intent, conn, BIND_EXTERNAL_SERVICE | ...)` on another
package: that package's service now executes inside a process with the app's UID and data directory — read
what it does, where its code comes from, and whether the peer is signature-verified (D06-020). (b) The app
declares `<service android:isolatedProcess="true" android:externalService="true" android:exported="true">`: any
caller can run it as themselves — the service must assume a hostile host; look for it trusting its own package
context (`getPackageName()`, files, prefs) as if it were the app's.
items.how:
```bash
grep -rn 'BIND_EXTERNAL_SERVICE\|BIND_EXTERNAL_SERVICE_LONG' "$DEC/jadx/sources" -B6 -A6
grep -nE 'externalService="true"' -B4 -A6 "$DEC/apktool/AndroidManifest.xml"
adb shell ps -AZ | grep -E 'isolated_app|com.target.app'   # (a): a peer's class name under the app's UID
```
items.proof:
(a) `ps -AZ`/`dumpsys activity processes` showing a process of the app's UID whose running service
class belongs to another package, plus the bind site with the flag and no signature check. (b) The probe
binding the app's external service with the flag and the service performing an app-scoped action under the
probe's UID.
items.escalation:
(a) → D17 (foreign code in the app's sandbox), D11 (its data). (b) → whatever the service trusts
about its host.
items.ruled_out_when:
No `BIND_EXTERNAL_SERVICE` bind targets a package outside the app's signing identity
(verified with `hasSigningCertificate` before the bind), and no `externalService="true"` service is declared.
